planting.note: Plant offsets or container specimens in leafy, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in deep shade, ideally mimicking the mossy rock crevices and streamside forest of its native Mpumalanga and Limpopo escarpment habitat; unlike other clivias it develops a true elongating stem over years and resents disturbance to its roots.

directions: Grow in deep, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full shade, ideally against a sheltered wall, tree trunk, or mossy bank where its lax, arching stems can be appreciated. Clivia caulescens is unique among the widely grown clivia species for developing a true visible stem that lengthens and can eventually lean or scramble over years, giving mature clumps a distinctive shrubby, almost bamboo-like presence quite unlike the stemless rosettes of C. miniata. Pendulous umbels of narrow, tubular, orange-red flowers with green tips appear in late summer to autumn rather than the typical late-winter clivia bloom season, extending the flowering window for a shade garden or collector's planting. Native to cool, high-altitude, mist-belt forest margins and rocky streambanks of the Drakensberg escarpment, it appreciates more consistent moisture and cooler root conditions than lowland clivia species and is slower to establish. Avoid disturbing the roots or stem base once planted, since recovery is slow.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown clumps in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full to part shade; unlike most clivias, robust clivia tolerates periodically waterlogged soil, reflecting its native swamp-forest habitat, and does not require the strict dry winter rest that most other species demand.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full to part shade; robust clivia was only formally separated from Clivia gardenii in 2004 and is the largest-growing of the pendulous-flowered clivia species, forming substantial clumps of broad, strap-shaped, glossy leaves considerably bigger than C. gardenii. Nodding umbels of tubular orange to orange-red flowers with yellow-green tips appear in late winter to spring, followed by large berries that ripen slowly over many months and are often still coloring as the next flush of flowers opens. Native to swampy, seasonally flooded coastal forest and riverine thicket of the Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal, it is unusually tolerant of wet, poorly drained soil for a clivia and does not need the pronounced dry winter rest that most other species require to flower well, though it still benefits from reduced watering in cooler months. A vigorous, garden-worthy choice for damp, deeply shaded sites such as low spots under tree canopy where standard clivia would struggle.
sources: SANBI Red List of South African Plants

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full shade; Belgian Hybrid strains were bred over decades in Belgium for broader petals and larger, more densely packed flower umbels than wild-type Clivia miniata, and are the form most commonly sold as flowering pot plants.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full shade to bright indirect light, keeping roots somewhat pot-bound to encourage flowering. Belgian Hybrid clivia refers to the strain of Clivia miniata developed by Belgian nurseries over generations of selective breeding for exceptionally large, rounded, overlapping petals and tightly packed, symmetrical umbels of 15-20 or more flowers, distinctly showier than the narrower-petaled wild species and the seed strain most widely distributed through the florist and houseplant trade worldwide. Flower color ranges from vivid orange to orange-red with a contrasting yellow throat, produced on sturdy scapes above broad, dark, strap-shaped evergreen leaves in late winter to spring. Like all clivia, it flowers most reliably after a 6-8 week cool, dry winter rest (roughly 50-55F with minimal watering); resume regular watering once a flower stalk becomes visible in the leaf axils. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since Belgian Hybrids bloom best when slightly crowded, and disturbance can delay flowering for a year or more.
